d1.purpose: Present a ranked excerpt of the world's tallest buildings, with measurements, locations, completion years and contextual notes.
tasks: Find a building by rank or name and read across to its attributes.
Compare heights and floor counts in rank order.
Locate buildings by city or country and check their completion years.
Read comments for records and other distinctions.
relations: Rank, name, height, floors, location, year and comments belong to the same building.
Metres and feet are two representations of the same height and share a grouped header.
City and country together identify a building's location.
The displayed ranks skip 9; the excerpt should not be read as a continuous sequence.
roles: The first column identifies rank; the name column identifies the building.
Height and floor columns support quantitative comparison.
City, country and year supply location and chronological context.
Comments provide secondary narrative detail; blank comments are meaningful empty cells.
The two-level header groups the height units while the other headers span both header rows.
keep_whole: Rank, height values, floor counts and years should remain intact wherever space allows.
Individual words in names, places and comments should remain intact.
The association between each floor count and its below-ground qualification should remain clear.
may_wrap: Building names, multiword cities and countries may wrap at word boundaries.
Floor qualifications may wrap after the main count or between words.
Comments may wrap into several lines at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: The two height-unit columns should have similar widths sufficient for their values.
Compact rank and year columns should reflect their short, consistent contents.
Name and location columns need room for identifiers; comments need more room for prose.
d1.h_vs_v: A 359px table forces breaks within numbers and words and makes rows very tall because nine columns each carry 21px of padding and border. Scrolling preserves readable units and denser rows, but requires horizontal movement to connect names with locations and comments.

d2.purpose: Present a ranked reference list of the world's tallest buildings and their distinguishing facts.
tasks: Identify a building and its rank.
Find a building's city, country and completion year.
Read comments for records and other distinctions.
relations: Rank and name identify each entry; height in metres and feet gives two measures of the same quantity.
City, country and year locate the building in place and time.
Comments qualify or explain the building's significance.
roles: The blank first header labels the rank column.
Name is the principal lookup column.
Height groups the metre and foot subcolumns; floors is a related quantitative field.
City, country and year provide compact reference fields; comments contain variable-length prose.
keep_whole: Individual words in names, places and comments where space permits.
Floor counts and their parenthetical qualifiers where practical.
may_wrap: Multiword cities and countries at word spaces.
Floor qualifiers and comments at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: The two height subcolumns should have similar widths.
Rank and year are compact reference fields; city and country merit comparable, moderately wider space.
d2.h_vs_v: A 359px table forces words and numbers to split and makes rows exceptionally tall. Scrolling preserves legibility and supports comparison, at the cost of moving horizontally to reach location and commentary.

d3.purpose: Present a ranked reference list of the world's tallest buildings, with comparable measurements, locations, completion years and distinguishing notes.
tasks: Find a building by rank or name.
Compare heights and floor counts across buildings.
Identify each building's location and completion year.
Read comments for records and other context.
relations: Rank, name and both height units identify and compare the same building.
The m and ft columns are paired under the Height header.
City and country form a location; floor counts may include a parenthetical count of below-ground floors.
Comments qualify the building in the same row and vary greatly in length.
roles: The first column is the rank, although its header is blank.
Names serve as practical row identifiers.
Height, floors and year are compact factual fields; city and country are location fields.
Comments are variable-length prose; the two-level height header groups equivalent measurements.
keep_whole: Ranks, height values, floor-count numbers and years.
Individual words in names, locations, headers and comments.
The m and ft unit labels.
may_wrap: Building names and multiword locations at word boundaries.
Floor-count annotations at word boundaries, while keeping their association with the count clear.
Comments as prose at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: The two height columns should have similar widths.
Compact numeric fields should generally be narrower than names and prose, subject to their headers and values.
City and country should have comparable prominence, with room for their different content lengths.
d3.h_vs_v: At phone width, preserving whole words and numbers across all nine columns is impossible with the fixed padding; a fitted table becomes very tall and breaks semantic units. Scrolling permits legible fields and shorter rows, but readers must move horizontally to connect names with later columns and comments.

analysis.strengths: All headers and words remain intact. Rank, name and both height units fit in the initial viewport, and the table is the narrowest of the scrolling layouts.
analysis.faults: Several names and place names wrap, while three-line comments make some rows tall. The initial viewport cuts through the Floors column, and substantial horizontal scrolling is needed to reach the comments.
analysis.spatial_logic: It protects the compact numeric fields and full floor descriptions, then uses a moderate name width and a relatively narrow comments column to limit total width.

analysis.strengths: The entire grid fits the viewport without horizontal scrolling. Its slightly wider comments column makes it shorter than S.
analysis.faults: Names, numbers, headers and comments break into fragments. The very tall rows make comparison and continuous reading difficult, despite the complete grid being on screen.
analysis.spatial_logic: It distributes almost all columns equally, with a small extra allowance for comments. That distribution bears little relation to the lengths or functions of their contents.

analysis.strengths: Words and headers stay intact, comments occupy at most two lines, and the table has the shortest and most consistent rows. Rank, name and both height units are visible initially.
analysis.faults: It requires the most horizontal scrolling. Some names and places wrap, and the 400px comments column makes the table substantially wider than the viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: It gives comments the largest allocation to control row height, while keeping floor descriptions on one line and using narrower place columns.

analysis.strengths: The entire grid fits the viewport, and the name column is slightly wider than in Q.
analysis.faults: Text and numeric values fragment throughout. Narrower comments produce even taller rows than Q, making the table exceptionally difficult to scan.
analysis.spatial_logic: It shifts a few pixels from comments to names within an otherwise nearly equal-width grid. That small gain for names is outweighed by the increased wrapping elsewhere.

analysis.strengths: The initial viewport contains rank, both height units and more complete names than P or R. Place names wrap less, and all words and headers remain intact.
analysis.faults: Three-line comments create taller rows than R, while the table still requires extensive horizontal scrolling. The longest names and United Arab Emirates still wrap.
analysis.spatial_logic: It prioritizes the first-screen lookup task by making the first four columns total 359px, then gives places more room and comments less room than R.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve the information far better: the first screen can pair building names with both height measures, while later columns remain reachable by scrolling. R's wider comments reduce row height; T's wider names and places improve lookup and reduce wrapping in those fields. At 360px, nine padded columns cannot accommodate their content naturally: Q is the better fitting example, but both fitting layouts fragment so much text that neither is a satisfactory reading experience.

analysis.strengths: The initial viewport contains rank, readable building names and both height units. Headers and numeric values remain whole, and comments wrap naturally in at most two lines.
analysis.faults: The table requires substantial horizontal scrolling. Long names and the United Arab Emirates wrap, and the wide floors and comments columns place later fields far from the names.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width favors the primary comparison at first sight, then gives explanatory text enough room to keep rows relatively compact.

analysis.strengths: Both height columns retain readable values, and the overall width is close to the viewport.
analysis.faults: Most other columns break words and even years into fragments. Extremely tall rows destroy scanning and comparison, while the table still requires horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: Protecting the height columns leaves too little width for nearly every other field; a small horizontal saving produces a severe vertical cost.

analysis.strengths: Rank, names and both height units are visible initially; all words remain intact. It saves some horizontal distance relative to s0A.
analysis.faults: Several names, cities and countries wrap more often, adding height and interrupting place-name lookup. A sliver of the floors column appears at the viewport edge without conveying useful information.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrower identity and location columns trade reading continuity for a modest reduction in scrolling.

analysis.strengths: Its initial view preserves the same useful rank, name and height comparison as s0A. Words remain whole, and the shorter comments column reduces horizontal scrolling.
analysis.faults: Long comments reach three lines and make several rows noticeably taller, leaving large blank areas in the initial viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: It concentrates the width reduction in prose rather than identifiers, but the resulting row-height changes weaken the rhythm of the whole table.

analysis.strengths: It fits the viewport and gives comments more room than the other narrow columns.
analysis.faults: Headers, names, measurements, years and prose fragment extensively. The very tall rows make lookup and comparison impractical despite the absence of horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: Distributing almost all available width evenly leaves every column below its content needs; the extra comment width cannot rescue the grid.

rounds.insights: s0A provides the strongest scrolling layout: the first screen supports the central rank-and-height comparison, while the full table remains readable. R and T show that modest width savings can create extra wrapping and taller rows. Q is the only fitting candidate, but it demonstrates that a usable nine-column table is not achievable at this viewport under the fixed typography and padding; any fitting refinement is necessarily a severe compromise.

analysis.strengths: Names and both height units are visible together in the initial viewport. Text wraps without breaking words, and the rows have a consistent rhythm.
analysis.faults: The narrow Floors column forces every floor entry onto two lines, making even short records taller. Most other fields require horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The initial viewport is well allocated to rank, name and height, but the uniform row height is largely imposed by repeated wrapping in one column.

analysis.strengths: The wider Floors column keeps its entries on one line, while the initial viewport retains the useful rank–name–height comparison. Words remain intact.
analysis.faults: The narrower Comments column makes the long seventh-row comment three lines, producing a conspicuously tall row with mostly empty space elsewhere.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width moves from comments to floor counts, improving many rows but creating one pronounced interruption in the vertical rhythm.

analysis.strengths: All columns are present within the viewport, and the name column has slightly more space than in Q.
analysis.faults: Headers, numbers and words fragment extensively; rows become extremely tall and cross-row comparison is impractical. The measured 410 breaks inside words are a severe readability failure.
analysis.spatial_logic: The small widths distribute space across all fields but leave none of the text-heavy columns enough room for continuous reading.

analysis.strengths: The initial viewport shows rank, mostly intact names and both height units together. Floors stay on one line, comments use at most two lines, and no words are broken.
analysis.faults: The full table is wide, so reading city, country, year and comments requires substantial horizontal scrolling. Two long names wrap, and the first country wraps.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width is assigned according to content: compact numeric columns, a generous name column, single-line floor entries and enough comment space to avoid the unusually tall row in s1B. Varied row heights reflect actual content.

analysis.strengths: The wider Comments column reduces the overall height and maximum cell line count relative to s1C.
analysis.faults: Names, measurements, headers and comments still break into fragments; 415 inside-word breaks make lookup and comparison very difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: Moving width from Name to Comments shortens some rows, but it trades away identification for a modest improvement in an already unreadable fit-to-viewport layout.

rounds.insights: s0A is the strongest scrolling layout: its first view supports the central rank, name and height task, while its wider Floors and Comments columns keep the full table readable. The fitting examples demonstrate that equal or near-equal widths cannot accommodate this content at 360 px; reducing height alone does not make the fragments readable. A fitting refinement can test whether prioritizing names improves identification, but it cannot preserve all semantic units within the available width.

analysis.strengths: All text and headers remain intact, with no measured breaks inside words. The initial viewport presents rank, name, and both height units together. Floor counts stay on one line.
analysis.faults: The seventh building’s comment occupies three lines, making its row noticeably taller. City, country, year, and comments require substantial horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first 359 px are devoted to the primary ranking and height comparison; generous widths beyond that preserve floor-count and comment readability.

analysis.strengths: Keeps the same useful first-screen comparison as s2A, with intact words and single-line headers. The slightly wider comments column reduces the tallest cell to two lines and removes the conspicuously tall seventh-building row.
analysis.faults: The table is 878 px wider than the viewport, so looking up location, year, or comments requires extensive scrolling. Some rows are tall because of content outside the initial viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: A small increase in comment width produces a more even vertical rhythm while preserving the compact first-screen grouping of rank, name, and height.

analysis.strengths: All columns fit within the phone viewport, so no horizontal scrolling is needed.
analysis.faults: Words, numbers, names, and headers fragment extensively. The exceptionally tall rows make comparison and continuous reading impractical, even though the table fits horizontally.
analysis.spatial_logic: Near-equal narrow columns distribute width without regard to content, forcing long text into extreme vertical stacks.

rounds.insights: s0A is the stronger scrolling design: a 10 px increase in comments removes a third line without disturbing the useful first viewport. Q shows that fitting every column is insufficient when the available text widths destroy semantic units. A fitted alternative should assign width by reading priority, though substantial fragmentation is unavoidable at 360 px.

bad.why: Words, numbers and headers break into fragments, creating extremely tall rows; it also requires scrolling despite its narrow columns.
Names, measurements and headers break inside words and numbers, and the table still extends beyond the viewport.
Fitting the viewport comes at the cost of fragmented names, measurements and prose, with rows hundreds of pixels tall.

contrast.why: An equal-width allocation appears orderly and fits the viewport, but gives names and comments almost no usable text width and splits measurements and words across lines.

sameFunctionGroups.why: Metres and feet are paired representations of height; their similar content widths support nearly equal columns.
City and country are related location fields and can use a comparable scale, adjusted for their different name lengths.

synthesis.rationale: s0A keeps the rank, building name and both height units visible together initially, with natural wrapping and compact rows. Layout Q is the best of the fitting candidates by its shorter overall height, but its fragmented text and numbers make it unsuitable for publication; it is included only to represent the required fitting class. The other scrolling layouts preserve readable text, though narrower names or comments create more wrapping.

general: Protect complete words, numbers and identifiers before optimizing for compactness.
Size columns for their content and lookup role rather than distributing width equally.
Evaluate the first viewport as well as the complete scrollable table.
specific: Keeping rank, name and both height units together in the initial viewport supports the table's primary comparison task.
The long comments need substantially more width than the numerical height fields.
At this viewport and fixed typography, the fitting candidates sacrifice basic readability.

synthesis.tradeoffs: s0A requires substantial horizontal scrolling to reach location, year and comments. Layout Q avoids horizontal scrolling but makes nearly every field difficult to read and greatly increases vertical scrolling.
synthesis.uncertain: Layout Q is a relative choice between two unacceptable fitting candidates; neither should be approved for publication under the stated readability criteria. Actual scrolling usability also depends on interaction details not shown in the static renders.
